ANA is highly sensitive but nonspecific. Anti-histone suggests drug-induced lupus, and anti-Ro is associated with photosensitivity and subacute cutaneous lupus.

q: A 62-year-old man presents with progressive, painless jaundice and 8 kg weight loss over 2 months. Examination reveals a non-tender, palpable gallbladder. Liver function tests show obstructive pattern. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Carcinoma of the head of pancreas
ex: Painless progressive jaundice with a palpable, non-tender gallbladder in an older patient with weight loss is classic of carcinoma of the head of pancreas (Courvoisier's law). Gallstone disease typically causes pain and a tender gallbladder; gallbladder carcinoma usually presents with a mass and late jaundice.

q: A 32-year-old G2P1 at 32 weeks gestation presents with sudden, painless, bright red vaginal bleeding. Her uterus is soft and nontender, fetal heart rate is 140/min, and the presenting part is high. What is the most appropriate next investigation?
o: Digital vaginal examination to assess the cervix
ex: Painless, bright red bleeding in the third trimester with a soft, nontender uterus and high presenting part suggests placenta previa. Digital vaginal examination is contraindicated as it may precipitate torrential hemorrhage; ultrasonography confirms placental location and is the investigation of choice.

q: An 8-month-old infant presents with episodic screaming, drawing up of legs, and passage of blood-stained stools described as "currant jelly." Examination reveals a sausage-shaped mass in the right upper quadrant. Abdominal ultrasound confirms intussusception with no evidence of perforation or peritonitis. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Air enema reduction under fluoroscopic or ultrasound guidance
Observation with oral fluids and analgesia
ex: Classic triad (colicky pain, currant jelly stool, sausage-shaped mass) suggests intussusception, commonest 6-18 months. Air enema is both diagnostic and therapeutic in uncomplicated cases (no perforation/peritonitis), with success >80%. Laparotomy is reserved for failed pneumatic reduction or signs of peritonitis/perforation.

q: A 26-year-old man with schizophrenia on depot haloperidol presents with fever (40°C), severe muscle rigidity, altered consciousness, and autonomic instability. Investigations reveal serum CK 28,000 U/L and leukocytosis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
ex: NMS is an idiosyncratic reaction to antipsychotics (potent D2 blockade), classically with rigidity, hyperthermia, altered sensorium, autonomic instability, and markedly elevated CK. Management: stop antipsychotic, supportive care, dantrolene/bromocriptine. Serotonin syndrome (rapid onset, myoclonus, diarrhea, history of SSRIs), malignant hyperthermia (post-anesthesia, succinylcholine/volatile agents), and catatonia (no fever, normal CK) are excluded.

q: A 22-year-old man undergoing emergency laparotomy under general anaesthesia (sevoflurane, succinylcholine) develops masseter spasm, tachycardia, rising end-tidal CO2, and metabolic acidosis 20 minutes after induction. Temperature is 38.5°C. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
o: Dantrolene sodium 2.5 mg/kg IV, repeated as needed
ex: Features indicate malignant hyperthermia (triggered by volatile agents and succinylcholine; early signs include masseter spasm, rising ETCO2, tachycardia, acidosis). Definitive treatment is IV dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg (oral form is for prophylaxis, not acute crisis). Stop triggers, hyperventilate with 100% O2, cool, correct acidosis.

q: A 45-year-old man with a history of blunt abdominal trauma presents with pain and hematuria. An urgent CT of the abdomen shows a wedge-shaped area of decreased parenchymal enhancement in the left kidney with a peripheral enhancing rim (cortical rim sign) and no contrast excretion into the collecting system. Which vascular injury is most likely?
ex: Cortical rim sign (rim of preserved subcapsular enhancement) with a non-enhancing, non-excreting kidney indicates renal artery thrombosis/occlusion — the rim is supplied by capsular collaterals. Dissection shows an intimal flap; pseudoaneurysm shows focal contrast pooling; AV fistula shows early venous enhancement.

q: A 22-year-old man sustains a fall onto an outstretched hand. On examination, he has a dinner-fork deformity of the wrist. Plain radiographs show a dorsally displaced, dorsally angulated fracture of the distal radius with associated fracture of the ulnar styloid. Which of the following is the most appropriate diagnosis?
ex: Colles fracture is a fracture of the distal radius with dorsal displacement and dorsal angulation (dinner-fork deformity), typically from a fall on an outstretched hand. Smith fracture has volar displacement/angulation (garden-spade deformity). Barton fracture is an intra-articular marginal shearing fracture of the distal radius (volar or dorsal). Die-punch fracture is an intra-articular depression of the lunate fossa of the distal radius.

q: A 35-year-old woman presents with painful oral erosions followed by flaccid blisters on the scalp and trunk. Nikolsky sign is positive, and a Tzanck smear of a blister base shows acantholytic cells. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
ex: Pemphigus vulgaris: intraepidermal (suprabasal) acantholysis, flaccid blisters, positive Nikolsky sign, oral involvement common, Tzanck smear shows acantholytic cells; caused by IgG autoantibodies against desmoglein 3. Bullous pemphigoid causes subepidermal tense blisters in older adults with negative Nikolsky; dermatitis herpetiformis is pruritic grouped vesicles with granular IgA deposits; epidermolysis bullosa is a hereditary blistering disorder with blisters at sites of trauma.

q: A 45-year-old man develops foot drop and inability to dorsiflex the foot after prolonged squatting. Sensation is impaired over the dorsum of the foot, but plantar flexion and inversion of the foot are preserved. Which nerve is most likely injured?
o: Deep branch of the femoral nerve
ex: The common peroneal (fibular) nerve winds around the neck of the fibula, where it is vulnerable to compression during prolonged squatting or crossed-leg sitting. It supplies the dorsiflexors (tibialis anterior, via deep peroneal) and foot everters (superficial peroneal); injury causes foot drop with sensory loss over the dorsum of the foot. Plantar flexion (triceps surae) and inversion (tibialis posterior) are tibial nerve functions and remain intact.

q: A 3-week-old infant presents with jaundice, hepatosplenomegaly, and bilateral cataracts. Urine is positive for a reducing substance, but glucose oxidase (dipstick) test is negative. Deficiency of which enzyme is the most likely cause?
ex: Classic galactosemia is due to deficiency of galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase (GALT). Galactose is metabolized to galactitol by aldose reductase in the lens, causing osmotic damage and cataracts. The urine contains a reducing sugar (galactose) that is not detected by glucose oxidase dipstick. Galactokinase deficiency causes only cataracts without liver disease.

q: A 26-year-old woman with chronic iron deficiency anemia (Hb 7 g/dL) is asymptomatic at rest. Which adaptation in her erythrocytes facilitates oxygen delivery to tissues?
o: Left shift of the oxygen–hemoglobin dissociation curve
Increased intra-erythrocytic 2,3-BPG causing a rightward shift of the curve
Increased affinity of hemoglobin for oxygen
Decreased cardiac output to reduce oxygen consumption
ex: In anemia, tissue hypoxia stimulates increased 2,3-BPG synthesis in RBCs. 2,3-BPG binds deoxyhemoglobin, decreasing O2 affinity and right-shifting the O2–Hb dissociation curve, which enhances O2 unloading at tissues. A left shift or increased Hb-O2 affinity would impair unloading; cardiac output actually increases in anemia to maintain oxygen delivery.

q: A 28-year-old man presents with painless cervical lymphadenopathy, intermittent fever, and weight loss. Excisional biopsy of a lymph node shows large binucleated cells with prominent eosinophilic nucleoli (owl-eye appearance) in a mixed inflammatory background. Which immunophenotype is most characteristic of these neoplastic cells?
o: CD15 positive, CD30 positive, CD45 (LCA) negative
ex: The cells are Reed-Sternberg cells of classical Hodgkin lymphoma (CHL). They classically express CD15 and CD30, are negative for CD45 (LCA) and usually CD20, and arise from germinal center B cells; association with EBV is common.

q: A 65-year-old man with atrial fibrillation on digoxin presents with nausea, vomiting, and yellow-tinted vision. ECG shows frequent premature ventricular complexes. Serum digoxin level is 3.4 ng/mL (therapeutic: 0.8–2.0 ng/mL). Which of the following is the definitive treatment?
ex: Digoxin immune Fab binds and neutralizes digoxin, removing it from Na+/K+-ATPase, and treats all features of toxicity (GI, visual, arrhythmic). Lidocaine and phenytoin only suppress digoxin-induced arrhythmias without clearing the drug. Potassium is contraindicated — digoxin toxicity causes hyperkalemia, and giving potassium may be fatal.

q: A 35-year-old man with HIV infection (CD4 count 40 cells/µL) presents with fever and headache of 2 weeks' duration. CSF examination shows lymphocytic pleocytosis, elevated protein, and low glucose. India ink preparation reveals budding yeast cells surrounded by a wide clear halo. Which of the following is the MOST likely causative organism?
ex: Cryptococcus neoformans is the most common cause of fungal meningitis in AIDS patients (CD4 < 100). The wide clear halo on India ink is its thick polysaccharide capsule, the principal virulence factor (antiphagocytic). CSF shows lymphocytic pleocytosis with low glucose. Pneumococcus and meningococcus cause acute pyogenic meningitis with polymorphonuclear pleocytosis; Listeria causes acute/subacute meningitis in immunocompromised and neonates.

q: A 22-year-old man with a history of intravenous drug use is brought to the emergency department unconscious. Examination: respiratory rate 6/min, blood pressure 90/60 mmHg, pinpoint pupils, and needle-track marks over both antecubital fossae. Which drug is the most likely cause of his presentation?
ex: Classic opioid (heroin) toxidrome: coma, respiratory depression, and pinpoint (miotic) pupils, with needle-track marks supporting IV opioid abuse. Cocaine and amphetamine cause mydriasis, tachycardia, and agitation; LSD causes hallucinations and mydriasis. Opioid overdose is reversed by naloxone.

q: A Pap smear-based screening test for cervical carcinoma has a sensitivity of 95% and specificity of 95%. When applied to a population with a disease prevalence of 10%, the positive predictive value (PPV) of the test is approximately:
ex: PPV = TP / (TP + FP). In 1000 women with 10% prevalence: 100 diseased → 95 true positives (95% sensitivity); 900 non-diseased → 45 false positives (5% of 900). PPV = 95 / (95 + 45) = 95/140 ≈ 68%. PPV falls with decreasing prevalence, unlike sensitivity/specificity.

q: A 25-year-old man presents with recurrent, self-limited right-sided nosebleeds, worse in winter, that stop with local pressure. Bleeding is seen from the anterior part of the nasal septum on examination. Which structure is the most common source of such anterior epistaxis?
o: Woodruff's plexus over the posterior lateral nasal wall
Kiesselbach's plexus (Little's area) on the anteroinferior nasal septum
The anterior ethmoidal artery at the superior septum
The sphenopalatine artery at the posterior choana
ex: Kiesselbach's plexus (Little's area), where branches of the sphenopalatine, greater palatine, superior labial and anterior ethmoidal arteries anastomose, is the most common site of epistaxis (~90%), especially in young patients. Anterior bleeds typically respond to pressure and chemical cautery; posterior bleeds (Woodruff's plexus) occur in older patients and need packing.

q: A 60-year-old man presents with sudden, painless loss of vision in the right eye since 2 hours. Examination: visual acuity = perception of light, right pupil sluggishly reactive with relative afferent pupillary defect, and fundus shows diffuse retinal whitening with a cherry-red spot at the fovea. The most likely diagnosis is:
ex: Sudden painless vision loss with cherry-red spot at fovea and diffuse retinal whitening is classic for CRAO. The fovea appears red because the underlying choroid is visible through the thin foveal retina, while the inner retina is infarcted and opaque. A RAPD is present. CRVO shows diffuse retinal hemorrhages ("blood and thunder"); AION causes disc swelling with altitudinal field defect; retinal detachment causes a detached retina with retinal tear, not a cherry-red spot.

q: A 28-year-old woman presents with fever, sore throat, and malaise for 10 days. Examination reveals bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy, pharyngeal erythema, and splenomegaly. Peripheral smear shows many atypical lymphocytes, and the heterophile antibody test is positive. What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Infectious mononucleosis due to Epstein-Barr virus
ex: Fever, sore throat, lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, atypical lymphocytes, and a positive heterophile antibody test are classic features of EBV infectious mononucleosis. CMV and HIV cause mononucleosis-like illness but are typically heterophile-negative. ALL presents with blasts and cytopenias, not atypical lymphocytes.

q: A 58-year-old man presents with colicky central abdominal pain of 2 days' duration, bilious vomiting, absolute constipation and abdominal distension. He had undergone appendicectomy 20 years ago. Erect abdominal X-ray shows multiple air-fluid levels in a step-ladder pattern. What is the most likely cause of his obstruction?
ex: Adhesions from previous surgery are the commonest cause of small bowel obstruction in adults (~75%). Prior laparotomy scar, colicky pain, vomiting, constipation and step-ladder air-fluid levels are classical. Gallstone ileus usually affects elderly women with no prior surgery; caecal carcinoma typically presents with anaemia or large bowel obstruction; hernia would show a palpable swelling.

q: A 28-year-old primigravida at 34 weeks gestation presents with headache, visual blurring, and epigastric pain. BP is 170/110 mmHg, urine protein 3+, platelets 70,000/mm³, and AST 120 U/L. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Expectant management with labetalol and weekly monitoring
IV magnesium sulfate prophylaxis followed by urgent delivery
Nifedipine alone and reassessment in 48 hours
ex: HELLP syndrome: hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes (AST 120), low platelets (70,000) in severe preeclampsia with epigastric pain. Definitive treatment is delivery regardless of gestational age; IV MgSO4 prevents seizures. Expectant management is contraindicated in HELLP; plasmapheresis is reserved for refractory/persistent postpartum cases.

q: A 3-year-old boy presents with progressive periorbital and pedal edema over 2 weeks and frothy urine. BP 90/60 mmHg. Urine shows protein 3+, no RBCs. Serum albumin 1.8 g/dL, total cholesterol 320 mg/dL. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
ex: Nephrotic syndrome at age 1-6 years is most often minimal change disease (steroid-sensitive). First-line therapy is oral prednisolone (60 mg/m²/day); cyclophosphamide and tacrolimus are reserved for steroid-dependent or frequently relapsing disease. IV albumin + diuretics are used only for severe edema, not as first-line treatment.

q: A 24-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by her family because she has been mute and immobile for 2 days. When her arm is lifted, it remains in the raised position (waxy flexibility); she resists passive movement and stares blankly without responding to commands. Vital signs and physical examination are normal. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
ex: Clinical picture (mutism, immobility, waxy flexibility, negativism) is catatonia. Benzodiazepines such as lorazepam are the first-line treatment and produce rapid resolution in most cases. ECT is reserved for catatonia refractory to benzodiazepines. Haloperidol is contraindicated as it can precipitate malignant catatonia. Fluoxetine has no role in acute catatonia.

q: A 20-year-old man with a strong family history of malignant hyperthermia (MH) requires emergency appendicectomy under general anaesthesia. Which agent must be avoided in this patient?
ex: Volatile inhalational agents (sevoflurane, isoflurane, desflurane, halothane) and succinylcholine are MH triggers; they must be avoided in susceptible patients. Propofol, nitrous oxide and opioids are safe. Dantrolene is the specific treatment for MH crisis.

q: A 25-year-old man is brought 6 hours after a road traffic accident with altered sensorium. Non-contrast CT head shows a biconvex (lens-shaped) hyperdense extra-axial collection in the right temporoparietal region that does not cross the cranial sutures. What is the most likely diagnosis?
ex: Epidural hematoma appears as a biconvex/lens-shaped hyperdense collection on NCCT, confined by suture lines because the dura is adherent to the inner table of the skull at the sutures. It typically results from middle meningeal artery injury in the temporal region and may follow a lucid interval. In contrast, subdural hematoma is crescentic and crosses sutures but not the midline.

q: A 25-year-old man falls on his outstretched right hand while playing cricket. He has tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox and mild wrist pain, but the initial wrist radiograph shows no obvious fracture. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Advise rest and review in 4 weeks if pain persists
Immobilize in a thumb spica cast and repeat radiograph in 2 weeks
Immediate open reduction and internal fixation
Emergency MRI of the wrist to confirm the diagnosis
ex: Clinical suspicion of scaphoid fracture. Initial radiograph is often normal; the fracture becomes visible only after 1-2 weeks due to bone resorption at the fracture line. The scaphoid has a retrograde blood supply (distal to proximal), making the proximal fragment prone to avascular necrosis if undisplaced fractures are left untreated. Standard practice: immobilize in a thumb spica cast and repeat X-ray in 10-14 days.

q: A 32-year-old woman presents with painful erosions on the oral mucosa for 3 weeks, followed by flaccid blisters over the trunk and groin. On examination, gentle rubbing of normal-appearing skin produces a blister (positive Nikolsky sign). A smear from the floor of a fresh blister shows acantholytic cells. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
ex: Pemphigus vulgaris is an autoimmune intraepidermal blistering disorder with IgG autoantibodies against desmoglein 1 and 3. It presents with flaccid blisters and mucosal erosions (oral involvement is often the first sign), a positive Nikolsky sign, and acantholytic cells on Tzanck smear. Bullous pemphigoid (elderly, tense blisters, subepidermal, Nikolsky negative), dermatitis herpetiformis (pruritic grouped vesicles on extensor surfaces, IgA-mediated, celiac disease association), and epidermolysis bullosa (inherited, blistering after minor trauma) do not fit this picture.

q: A 45-year-old man develops left foot drop and inability to dorsiflex or evert the foot after prolonged sitting with his legs crossed. Sensation is lost over the dorsum of the foot, but plantar flexion and sensation on the sole are normal. Which nerve is most likely injured?
ex: The common peroneal nerve winds around the fibular neck, where it is superficial and vulnerable to compression (e.g., habitual leg crossing). Injury causes foot drop with loss of dorsiflexion and eversion, plus sensory loss over the dorsum of the foot. Intact plantar flexion and sole sensation indicate tibial nerve sparing.

q: A 2-month-old infant presents with vomiting, failure to thrive, jaundice, and hepatomegaly. Examination reveals cataracts in both eyes. Urine testing shows a reducing substance that is NOT detected by glucose oxidase test strips. Deficiency of which enzyme is most likely responsible?
ex: Classic galactosemia is due to deficiency of galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase (GALT), causing accumulation of galactose-1-phosphate and galactose. Galactose is a reducing sugar detected by Benedict's test but not by glucose oxidase strips. Hallmarks: hepatomegaly, cataracts, failure to thrive, jaundice. Galactokinase deficiency causes only cataracts (galactitol deposition) without severe systemic illness.

q: A 65-year-old man with severe COPD has chronic CO2 retention (PaCO2 60 mm Hg, PaO2 55 mm Hg). His ventilatory drive is now maintained mainly by which of the following?
o: Central chemoreceptors responding to increased CSF H+ concentration
Peripheral chemoreceptors responding to decreased arterial PO2
Pulmonary stretch receptors responding to increased lung volume
Central chemoreceptors responding to increased CSF CO2 concentration
ex: In chronic hypercapnia, renal retention of HCO3- normalizes CSF pH, desensitizing central chemoreceptors to CO2. Ventilation is then maintained by the hypoxic drive: peripheral chemoreceptors (carotid bodies) respond to PaO2 < 60 mm Hg. Giving high-flow O2 may abolish this drive and cause CO2 narcosis.

q: A 45-year-old man presents with nephrotic syndrome. Renal biopsy shows amorphous eosinophilic material in the glomerular mesangium and basement membranes. This material stains with Congo red and shows apple-green birefringence under polarized light. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
ex: Apple-green birefringence on Congo red staining under polarized light is pathognomonic of amyloidosis. Amyloid deposits are amorphous eosinophilic extracellular material composed of misfolded fibrillar proteins (AL in primary/plasma cell dyscrasia, AA in chronic inflammation). Fibrillary glomerulonephritis mimics amyloid on light and electron microscopy but is Congo red negative. Minimal change disease shows no immune deposits and responds to steroids; membranous nephropathy shows subepithelial deposits with a spiked basement membrane on silver staining.

q: A 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus on metformin presents with worsening dyspnea. Echocardiography shows ejection fraction 30% (NYHA class III heart failure). Which of the following antidiabetic drugs is CONTRAINDICATED in this patient?
ex: Pioglitazone (a thiazolidinedione) causes fluid retention and plasma volume expansion, worsening heart failure; it is contraindicated in NYHA class III/IV heart failure. Empagliflozin (SGLT2 inhibitor) is actually beneficial in heart failure; sitagliptin (DPP-4 inhibitor) is neutral; glimepiride (sulfonylurea) is not contraindicated.

q: A 40-year-old man presents with profuse watery diarrhea and vomiting 12 hours after eating seafood at a coastal restaurant. Stool is pale, flecked with mucus and epithelial cells (rice-water appearance). He is dehydrated and in shock. Dark-field microscopy of a fresh stool smear shows darting, comma-shaped bacilli. Which is the most likely causative organism?
ex: Rice-water stools with rapid dehydration plus darting, comma-shaped Gram-negative bacilli on dark-field microscopy are classic for Vibrio cholerae. Cholera toxin ADP-ribosylates Gsα, causing constitutive adenylate cyclase activation and ↑cAMP, driving massive Cl⁻ and water secretion into the gut lumen. Treatment is aggressive rehydration; doxycycline shortens illness. ETEC causes traveler's diarrhea (less severe), Giardia causes malabsorptive stools with cysts/trophozoites, and rotavirus is a common cause of infantile diarrhea.

q: A dead body is examined about 6 hours after death. Rigor mortis would first be evident in which of the following muscle groups?
o: Small muscles of the face and eyelids
Large muscles of the lower limbs
Muscles of the back and abdomen
ex: Rigor mortis begins 1-2 hours after death, first affecting small muscles (eyelids, face, jaw) and progressing cephalocaudally to larger trunk and limb muscles (Nysten's law); it is fully developed by 12-24 hours and disappears in the same order by 24-48 hours. Cardiac muscle is not affected.

q: A new screening test for cervical cancer (sensitivity 80%, specificity 90%) is applied to 10,000 women with a disease prevalence of 2%. How many women will be false positives?
ex: Prevalence 2% of 10,000 = 200 diseased, 9,800 healthy. False positives = 10% (100 − specificity) of 9,800 = 980. True positives = 80% of 200 = 160; false negatives = 40; true negatives = 8,820.

q: A 28-year-old woman presents with gradually progressive bilateral hearing loss and tinnitus for 2 years. Otoscopic examination shows normal tympanic membranes bilaterally. Rinne test is negative on both sides and Weber test lateralizes to the left. Pure tone audiometry reveals bilateral conductive hearing loss with a Carhart's notch at 2 kHz. Her mother has similar hearing impairment. The most likely diagnosis is:
ex: Bilateral conductive hearing loss with intact tympanic membrane, positive family history (autosomal dominant) and Carhart's notch at 2 kHz are classic features of otosclerosis, caused by fixation of the stapes footplate. CSOM would show a tympanic membrane perforation; ototoxic drugs and presbycusis produce sensorineural, not conductive, loss.

q: A 58-year-old male with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes presents with sudden painless loss of vision in the right eye. Fundoscopy shows a clear vitreous, a pale retina with a cherry-red spot at the macula, and a box-car appearance of the blood column in the retinal vessels. What is the most likely diagnosis?
ex: Sudden painless visual loss with cherry-red spot at the macula (choroid visible through the thin fovea) and box-car (cattle-trucking) of vessels is classic for central retinal artery occlusion, an ophthalmic emergency. Retinal vein occlusion causes retinal hemorrhages and venous engorgement; ischemic optic neuropathy causes optic disc edema, not a cherry-red spot.

q: A 35-year-old woman presents with 2 weeks of fever, polyarthralgia of both ankles, and painful red nodules over the shins. Chest X-ray shows bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy with clear lung fields. Serum calcium is mildly elevated. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
ex: Erythema nodosum with bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy (BHL), fever, and ankle arthritis defines Lofgren syndrome, an acute form of sarcoidosis. BHL with clear lung fields on CXR is characteristic. Elevated ACE and hypercalcemia support the diagnosis; confirmed by non-caseating granulomas on biopsy. TB usually shows focal upper-zone infiltrates with unilateral hilar or paratracheal nodes; BHL with erythema nodosum favors sarcoidosis.

q: A 32-year-old woman with gallstones develops fever, jaundice, and right upper quadrant pain. Blood cultures grow E. coli. ERCP shows a stone impacted at the ampulla of Vater. Which intervention is most appropriate initially?
ex: This is ascending cholangitis (Charcot triad: pain, jaundice, fever). Urgent biliary decompression is required; endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) with sphincterotomy and stone extraction is the gold standard initial therapy. Cholecystectomy is deferred until cholangitis resolves.

q: A 32-week primigravida presents with sudden, painless, causeless vaginal bleeding. On examination, the uterus is soft and non-tender, and fetal heart sounds are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
ex: Painless, recurrent, causeless bleeding with a soft non-tender uterus and normal fetal heart sounds is classic of placenta previa, where the placenta implants in the lower segment. Abruptio placentae causes painful bleeding with a tense, tender (board-like) uterus and fetal distress. Vasa previa presents with bleeding plus fetal distress (often after membrane rupture). Uterine rupture causes severe abdominal pain, shock, and absent fetal heart sounds.

q: A 6-week-old male infant presents with projectile, non-bilious vomiting immediately after feeds for the past 1 week. He is alert but hungry. Examination reveals a palpable olive-shaped mass in the right upper quadrant. Blood gas analysis shows hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
ex: Projectile non-bilious vomiting in an infant aged 2-8 weeks with an olive-shaped pyloric mass and hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis is classic for infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis (IHPS). Duodenal atresia presents in neonates with bilious vomiting and a double-bubble sign on X-ray. Intussusception causes colicky pain with currant-jelly stools. Confirm IHPS with ultrasound (thickened pyloric muscle) and treat with Ramstedt pyloromyotomy.

q: A 19-year-old woman is brought by her family with 3 days of mutism, posturing, negativism, and waxy flexibility. She stares blankly and does not respond to commands. Which is the most appropriate immediate management?
ex: Clinical picture is catatonia (mutism, posturing, negativism, waxy flexibility). Benzodiazepines (lorazepam) are first-line; a lorazepam challenge is both diagnostic and therapeutic. Antipsychotics may worsen catatonia and precipitate neuroleptic malignant syndrome. ECT is reserved for benzodiazepine-resistant or malignant catatonia.

q: A 22-year-old man undergoing emergency laparotomy under general anaesthesia develops masseter muscle rigidity, tachycardia, and rapidly rising end-tidal CO2 within minutes of receiving suxamethonium and sevoflurane. Core temperature rises to 39.5°C over 30 minutes. What is the most appropriate immediate pharmacological management?
o: Dantrolene sodium 10 mg/kg IV as a single bolus
ex: Clinical picture = malignant hyperthermia (MH): triggered by suxamethonium and volatile anaesthetics; uncontrolled calcium release from sarcoplasmic reticulum via RyR1 receptor causes hypermetabolism (hypercapnia, rigidity, fever). Definitive treatment is dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg IV, repeated until control (up to 10 mg/kg cumulative). Stop trigger agents, hyperventilate with 100% O2, cool, correct acidosis and hyperkalaemia. Neostigmine only reverses non-depolarising blockers; nifedipine is contraindicated (risk of hyperkalaemia with dantrolene).

q: A 40-year-old woman presents with progressive dysphagia to both solids and liquids, and regurgitation of undigested food. Barium swallow shows smooth tapering of the distal esophagus with a "bird's beak" appearance. What is the most likely diagnosis?
ex: Achalasia is characterized by failure of relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter, producing a smooth, tapered "bird's beak" narrowing of the distal esophagus on barium swallow, with proximal dilation. Esophageal carcinoma causes an irregular, shouldered ("apple core") stricture; varices appear as serpiginous filling defects; hiatus hernia shows the gastroesophageal junction above the diaphragm.

q: A 65-year-old man with chronic renal failure on haemodialysis presents with acute severe pain in the left shoulder after lifting a light object. Radiograph shows displacement of the humeral head with a 'lightbulb sign'. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
ex: Posterior dislocation of shoulder ('lightbulb sign' on AP radiograph) is typical in seizure disorder and electrocution; chronic renal failure with renal osteodystrophy predisposes to it. Acute posterior dislocation is managed by closed reduction under anaesthesia with immobilisation; arthroplasty is reserved for chronic unreduced cases.

q: A 30-year-old man presents with well-demarcated erythematous plaques covered by silvery white scales over the elbows, knees, and scalp. Gentle scraping of a scale reveals pinpoint bleeding points (Auspitz sign). Nail pitting is noted. What is the most likely diagnosis?
ex: Silvery scales, Auspitz sign (pinpoint bleeding after scale removal), extensor distribution, and nail pitting are classical features of psoriasis, a chronic T-cell (Th17)-mediated dermatosis. Atopic dermatitis affects flexures with erythematous scaly patches and intense pruritus; lichen planus shows violaceous, polygonal, flat-topped papules with Wickham striae; pityriasis rosea presents as a herald patch followed by a Christmas-tree pattern of scaly macules on the trunk.

q: A 45-year-old man presents with pain and paresthesia over the medial aspect of the forearm and hand, and weakness of the ulnar nerve-innervated muscles, following a stab injury in the lower neck. Which anatomical structure has most likely been damaged?
o: Lower trunk of the brachial plexus
Upper trunk of the brachial plexus
Medial cord of the brachial plexus
Posterior cord of the brachial plexus
ex: The lower trunk (C8–T1) gives rise to the medial cord, which forms the ulnar nerve and the medial cutaneous nerves of the arm and forearm. Injury at the trunk level (as occurs in the lower neck) produces ulnar-type sensory loss and weakness of ulnar nerve-innervated muscles; the upper trunk (C5–C6) injury classically causes Erb palsy, and posterior cord injury affects the radial nerve distribution.

q: A 6-month-old infant presents with failure to thrive, cataracts, and hepatosplenomegaly. Urine shows a reducing substance that is negative on glucose oxidase testing. Which enzyme is most likely deficient?
ex: Classic galactosemia (classic type) is due to deficiency of galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase (GALT), causing cataracts, hepatosplenomegaly, and reducing sugar in urine that is not glucose (glucose oxidase test negative, unlike glucose). Galactokinase deficiency causes cataracts without other systemic features; glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency causes von Gierke disease (fasting hypoglycemia, lactic acidosis); epimerase deficiency is rare and milder.

q: A 25-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department 30 minutes after a road traffic accident with acute blood loss of about 2 L. She has tachycardia, cold clammy skin, and a blood pressure of 80/50 mmHg. The immediate physiological response responsible for her tachycardia and vasoconstriction is mediated by:
o: Increased sympathetic discharge via the baroreceptor reflex
ex: Acute hemorrhage lowers arterial pressure, reducing stretch on carotid sinus and aortic arch baroreceptors. Within seconds this triggers reflex sympathetic activation — tachycardia, peripheral vasoconstriction, cold clammy skin. ADH (minutes–hours) and RAAS (hours–days) are slower compensations; ANP levels fall, not rise, in hypovolemia.

q: A 22-year-old woman presents with painless left cervical lymphadenopathy, intermittent fever, and night sweats for 3 months. Excisional biopsy of the node shows large binucleate cells with prominent eosinophilic nucleoli (owl-eye appearance) in a background of small lymphocytes, eosinophils, and fibrosis. The neoplastic cells are positive for CD15 and CD30. The most likely diagnosis is:
ex: Binucleate Reed-Sternberg cells with owl-eye nucleoli in a mixed inflammatory background, with CD15+/CD30+ immunophenotype, are diagnostic of classical Hodgkin lymphoma. Nodular sclerosis is the most common subtype in young women, characterized by lacunar cells and dense fibrosis.

q: A 60-year-old man on digoxin for heart failure and atrial fibrillation presents with nausea, vomiting, yellow-tinted vision, and frequent ventricular ectopics on ECG. Serum digoxin level is 4.5 ng/mL. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
ex: Features suggest digoxin toxicity: GI symptoms, xanthopsia, arrhythmias, toxic level (>2 ng/mL). Digoxin immune Fab binds and inactivates digoxin; treatment of choice for life-threatening toxicity. Potassium is given only if hypokalemic (hypokalemia precipitates toxicity); lignocaine/phenytoin are adjuncts for arrhythmias, not definitive therapy.

q: A 62-year-old farmer presents with a 1-week history of fever, myalgia, and progressively ascending symmetric weakness of both lower limbs. Two weeks prior he sustained a penetrating nail injury to his foot while working in the fields. Neurological examination reveals areflexia and hypotonia; cerebrospinal fluid shows albuminocytologic dissociation (elevated protein, normal cell count). Which of the following is the most likely causative organism?
ex: Soil-contaminated wound + ascending flaccid paralysis + areflexia + albuminocytologic dissociation is classic Guillain-Barré syndrome, most commonly triggered by Campylobacter jejuni infection. C. botulinum causes descending flaccid paralysis with no sensory loss and normal CSF. C. tetani causes spastic paralysis (lockjaw, risus sardonicus). C. perfringens causes gas gangrene; C. difficile causes pseudomembranous colitis.

q: A 40-year-old farmer is brought dead to the emergency department. On examination: pinpoint pupils, profuse salivation, lacrimation, urinary and fecal incontinence, and a garlic-like odour on breath. The most likely poison and specific antidote are:
ex: Organophosphate compounds inhibit acetylcholinesterase, causing cholinergic excess: pinpoint (miotic) pupils, SLUDGE features (salivation, lacrimation, urination, defecation), and a garlic-like odour. Antidote: atropine (muscarinic antagonist) plus pralidoxime (reactivates the enzyme). Cyanide causes bitter-almond odour and cherry-red skin; atropine poisoning causes mydriasis, dry skin, and tachycardia.

q: A new rapid diagnostic test for malaria is evaluated against blood smear (gold standard) in 100 patients with fever. Results: 45 patients had both positive smear and positive rapid test; 5 patients had positive smear but negative rapid test; 10 patients had negative smear but positive rapid test; 40 patients had both tests negative. What is the sensitivity of the rapid test?
ex: Sensitivity = TP/(TP + FN) = 45/(45 + 5) = 90%. It measures the test's ability to correctly identify those with the disease; high sensitivity suits screening tests.

q: A 6-year-old boy presents with recurrent, painless, self-limiting epistaxis from the left nostril, worse during dry winter months. Examination is otherwise normal. The most common site of bleeding in this age group is:
o: Little's area (Kiesselbach's plexus) on the anterior nasal septum
Woodruff's plexus over the posterior end of the inferior meatus
The roof of the nasal cavity (olfactory region)
The anterior end of the inferior turbinate
ex: In children, epistaxis most often arises from Little's area, where branches of the sphenopalatine, anterior ethmoidal, greater palatine and superior labial arteries anastomose on the anteroinferior nasal septum; dry weather causes crusting and nose-picking trauma. Woodruff's plexus is a common site of posterior epistaxis in elderly patients.

q: A 60-year-old woman presents with severe pain, redness, and blurred vision in the right eye for 6 hours, with halos around lights. Examination shows corneal edema, a mid-dilated non-reacting pupil, shallow anterior chamber, and intraocular pressure of 55 mmHg. Which is the most appropriate immediate step in management?
ex: Acute angle-closure glaucoma is an ophthalmic emergency (IOP >40 mmHg, mid-dilated fixed pupil, corneal edema). Immediate management is medical IOP reduction with IV acetazolamide (carbonic anhydrase inhibitor) along with topical beta-blockers and hyperosmotics; pilocarpine is added after initial IOP lowering. Laser peripheral iridotomy is the definitive treatment, performed once the eye is soft and the cornea is clear.
